extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and researchers learning scheme-theoretic algebraic geometry
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, criteria, and local/global tests for scheme-theoretic image, reductions, (effective) Cartier divisors, regular sequences and regular embeddings, plus related constructions (cones, Veronese, rulings, fibered products) from a foundations-of-algebraic-geometry textbook chapter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of plane conics (char ≠ 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any plane conic (over an algebraically closed field of characteristic not 2) that can be written as the sum of three nonzero squares is isomorphic to P1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discusses the limited normal forms (sums of 3 squares, 2 squares, a single square, or 0) up to change of coordinates; see Exercise 6.5.F for a related fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree d rational normal curve (d-uple embedding)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proj S_d (for S = k[x,y]) is given by the 2×2 minors vanishing on the Hankel-like matrix of monomials; this scheme is rank 1 and is called the degree d rational normal curve in P^d.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the image of the d-uple (Veronese) embedding; the twisted cubic is the d = 3 case (Exercises 8.2.A and 8.2.F).

rubrics_metrics.name: d-uple (Veronese) embedding
rubrics_metrics.description: If S_• = k[x_0,...,x_n], then Proj S_•^{(d)} (the graded piece of degree d) gives a closed embedding Proj S^{(d)} ⊂ P^{N-1}, called the d-uple embedding or d-uple Veronese embedding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combining prior exercises shows Proj S^{(d)} is a closed embedding; N = dimension of homogeneous degree d polynomials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quadratic equations vanishing on the Veronese surface
rubrics_metrics.description: There exist six linearly independent quadratic equations vanishing on the Veronese surface Proj S_2 (S = k[x0,x1,x2]) sitting in P^5.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You needn't show they generate the full ideal here; hint suggests using the determinant identity of a 3×3 matrix of pairwise products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rulings on a smooth quadric surface
rubrics_metrics.description: A smooth rank-4 quadric surface X ⊂ P^3 (wz = xy) has two families (rulings) of lines, each parametrized by P^1; through every k-valued point of X passes exactly one line from each ruling; there are no other lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct lines via parametric points [a0c, b0c, a0d, b0d] as [c,d] varies in P^1; alternative approaches include algebraic manipulation or Bézout's theorem (Exercise 8.2.E). Over algebraically closed fields char ≠ 2 this identifies the quadric with P^1 × P^1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavior of linear spaces in maximal-rank quadrics
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is a maximal rank quadric hypersurface of dimension m, it contains no linear spaces of dimension greater than m/2; if m = 2a+1 then X contains an irreducible family of a-planes; if m = 2a then X contains two irreducible families of a-planes (rulings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This generalizes the two-ruling phenomenon of quadric surfaces to higher dimensions; see references for further discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighted projective space
rubrics_metrics.description: If variables x_i are given nonstandard degrees d_i, then Proj k[x_1,...,x_n] with those weights is weighted projective space P(d1,...,dn).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: P(m,n) ≅ P^1; P(1,1,2) ≅ Proj k[u,v,w,z]/(uw − v^2); think of these as projective cones over lower-dimensional projective varieties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affine cone of Proj S
rubrics_metrics.description: For a finitely generated graded ring S_•, the affine cone of Proj S_• is Spec S_•. (Terminology caution: this depends on the graded ring, not merely Proj S_•.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric intuition: Spec S_• is a cone with an origin point; removing the origin morally projects to Proj S_•. See exercises clarifying this projection and the distinguished open D(T) in the projective cone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Projective cone / projective completion
rubrics_metrics.description: The projective cone (projective completion) of Spec S_• is Proj S_•[T], where T is a new variable of degree 1; the closed subscheme T=0 corresponds to the projective part (Proj S_•) and D(T) is isomorphic to the affine cone Spec S_•.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This construction adjoins 'points at infinity' forming the Proj; useful for visualizing projective completions of affine cones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of scheme-theoretic image
rubrics_metrics.description: Given π : X → Y, the scheme-theoretic image is the smallest closed subscheme Z ⊂ Y such that the composition IZ/Y → OY → π_* OX is zero; equivalently the intersection of all closed subschemes containing the image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On affine Y = Spec B, the scheme-theoretic image is cut out by the ideal I(B) = ker(B → Γ(X, OX)). This notion captures nonreduced 'fuzz' of images and behaves better than naive set-theoretic images in general.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples illustrating scheme-theoretic image behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Several examples: (1) π: Spec k[ε]/(ε^2) → A^1 gives scheme-theoretic image Spec k[x]/(x^2) (fuzzy point); (2) π: Spec k[ε]/(ε^2) → A^1 sending ε ↦ 0 gives reduced image Spec k[x]/(x); (3) inclusion A^1 − {0} → A^1 has scheme-theoretic image A^1 (ideal zero) though set-theoretic image is A^1 − {0}; (4) pathological example where scheme-theoretic image is whole Y but set-theoretic image is a point (use inverse limit of fuzz).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These show that the scheme-theoretic image can have nonreduced structure and that its underlying set is closed (indeed the closure of the set-theoretic image under reasonable hypotheses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Affine-local criteria to compute scheme-theoretic images
rubrics_metrics.description: On an affine open Spec B ⊂ Y, define I(B) = ker(B → Γ(π^{-1}(Spec B), O_X)). The question: when does a function r/ g^n on D(g) that pulls back to zero lift to some m with r g^m pulling back to zero on Spec B? Three cases where the answer is yes: (i) π^{-1}(Spec B) reduced (take m=1), (ii) π^{-1}(Spec B) affine (use functions on localized affines), (ii') π^{-1}(Spec B) quasicompact (finite affine cover and take max m).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quasicompactness and reducedness are 'friends'; these local tests motivate Theorem 8.3.4.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 8.3.4 — affine-local computability of scheme-theoretic image
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose π : X → Y. If X is reduced or π is quasicompact, then the scheme-theoretic image of π may be computed affine-locally: on Spec A ⊂ Y it is cut out by the functions (elements of A) that pull back to the zero function on π^{-1}(Spec A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the key sufficient condition ensuring the scheme-theoretic image is the closed subscheme defined by the kernel ideals on affines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 8.3.5 — underlying set is closure of set-theoretic image
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the hypotheses of Theorem 8.3.4 (e.g., X reduced or π quasicompact), the closure of the set-theoretic image of π is the underlying set of the scheme-theoretic image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example 4 shows necessity of hypotheses: without them the underlying set of the scheme-theoretic image may differ drastically from the closure of the set-theoretic image.

rubrics_metrics.name: When set-theoretic image equals scheme-theoretic underlying set
rubrics_metrics.description: If the set-theoretic image is closed (for instance, if π is finite or projective), then the set-theoretic image is the underlying set of the scheme-theoretic image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful practical criterion: finite/projective morphisms have closed images, so no pathology arises in these cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scheme-theoretic closure of a locally closed subscheme
rubrics_metrics.description: The scheme-theoretic closure of a locally closed embedding π : X → Y is defined as the scheme-theoretic image of π (also called schematic closure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In quasicompact or reduced situations, this gives equivalence between several notions of locally closed embeddings (open of closed, closed of open, intersection).

rubrics_metrics.name: Induced reduced subscheme structure on a closed subset
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a closed subset X_set ⊂ Y, there is a canonical reduced scheme structure X on X_set obtained by cutting out functions that vanish at all points of X_set; on affine opens Spec B this corresponds to the radical ideal I(X_set).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternative constructions: as scheme-theoretic image of disjoint union of residue fields of points, or as the smallest closed subscheme whose underlying set contains X_set; exercises verify equivalence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction of a scheme (Y_red)
rubrics_metrics.description: The reduction Y_red of a scheme Y is the induced reduced closed subscheme with underlying set all of Y; on affine opens Spec B, Y_red corresponds to Spec B / nilradical N(B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduction 'shears off the fuzz' (nilpotents); equivalent descriptions via localization given in exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution: global sections modulo nilpotents need not equal sections of reduction
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not true that for every open U, Γ(U, O_Y) modulo its nilpotents equals Γ(U, O_{Y_red}). Example: Y = Spec k[x]/(x^n) where x is not globally nilpotent but is 0 on Y_red because it is 'locally nilpotent'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This warns against naive global computations of reductions; relates to earlier pathological Example 4.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of effective Cartier divisor (locally principal closed subschemes)
rubrics_metrics.description: A closed subscheme X ⊂ Y is locally principal if on a suitable open cover it is cut out by a single equation. It is an effective Cartier divisor if on an affine cover Spec A_i ⊂ Y the ideal of X|Spec A_i is generated by a non-zerodivisor t_i ∈ A_i.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalent: ideal sheaf is locally generated by a single non-zerodivisor. Hypotheses about affineness and generation discussed; see exercises for tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution: effectivity of Cartier divisors is not naively affine-local
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the effective Cartier divisor condition can be verified on an affine cover, it is not true that existence of a global t with D = V(t) holds in general; the condition is not an 'affine-local' condition in the obvious sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Exercise 19.11.10 and example 8.2.1 for flavor; verification requires care about covers and non-zerodivisors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization via associated points (locally Noetherian)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is a locally Noetherian scheme and t ∈ Γ(X, O_X), then V(t) is an effective Cartier divisor iff t does not vanish on any associated point of X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives a practical test in locally Noetherian situations to check that a principal closed subscheme is an effective Cartier divisor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness up to unit for local generators of effective Cartier divisors
rubrics_metrics.description: If V(t) = V(t') ⊂ Spec A is an effective Cartier divisor with t and t' non-zerodivisors in A, then t is an invertible function times t'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows local generators differ by units; useful for gluing local descriptions of divisors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of regular sequence for an A-module M
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence x_1,...,x_r ∈ A is an M-regular sequence if (i) for each i, x_i is not a zerodivisor on M/(x_1,...,x_{i-1})M, and (ii) (x_1,...,x_r)M ≠ M.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric intuition: successive effective Cartier divisors; regular sequences are the algebraic formalization of complete intersections locally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic properties of regular sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Regular sequences are stable under localization (Exercise 8.4.D); powers of elements can be arranged into regular sequences under hypotheses (Exercise 8.4.E); order matters in general but not in Noetherian local situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An illustrative example shows order can matter when the ring is not local (A = k[x,y,z]/(x−1)z).

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 8.4.6 — order-independence in Noetherian local rings
rubrics_metrics.description: If (A,m) is a Noetherian local ring and M a finitely generated A-module, then any M-regular sequence (x_1,...,x_r) contained in m remains a regular sequence upon any reordering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof reduces to the r=2 case via spectral-sequence/Koszul-type argument; Noetherian hypotheses are necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of regular embedding (locally closed embedding generated by regular sequence)
rubrics_metrics.description: A locally closed embedding π : X → Y is a regular embedding of codimension r at p ∈ X if the ideal of X in O_{Y,p} is generated by a regular sequence of length r. π is a regular embedding of codimension r if this holds at every p ∈ X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also called a local complete intersection in some contexts; codimension notion tied to Krull height theorems. Checking regular embedding is an open condition (Exercise 8.4.G).

rubrics_metrics.name: Openness and practical checking of regular embedding
rubrics_metrics.description: If a locally closed embedding of locally Noetherian schemes is a regular embedding at p, then it is a regular embedding in some open neighborhood of p. If X is quasicompact, to check a closed embedding is regular it suffices to check at closed points of X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algebraic reduction: reduce to affine case and use finiteness arguments (ideals I,J with I_p = J_p implies equality after inverting an element).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence: codimension 1 regular embeddings ↔ effective Cartier divisors
rubrics_metrics.description: A closed embedding X → Y of locally Noetherian schemes is a regular embedding of codimension 1 iff X is an effective Cartier divisor on Y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'effective Cartier divisor' ⇒ 'regular embedding of codimension 1' direction holds generally; the converse requires Noetherian-like hypotheses (OY coherent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of codimension r complete intersection
rubrics_metrics.description: A codimension r complete intersection in a scheme Y is a closed subscheme X that can be written as the scheme-theoretic intersection of r effective Cartier divisors D_1,...,D_r such that at every point p ∈ X the corresponding equations form a regular sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complete intersection means 'codimension r for some r'; ties together effective Cartier divisors and regular sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of fibered products of schemes
rubrics_metrics.description: For morphisms α : X → Z and β : Y → Z of schemes, the fibered product X ×_Z Y exists in the category of schemes (Theorem 9.1.1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notation caveats: people often write X ×_A B for base change; the fibered product satisfies the Yoneda/universal property Hom(W, X ×_Z Y) = Hom(W,X) ×_{Hom(W,Z)} Hom(W,Y).

rubrics_metrics.name: Warning: products of schemes are not necessarily products of underlying sets
rubrics_metrics.description: The underlying set of a scheme-theoretic product need not be the product of underlying sets; e.g., A^1_k ×_k A^1_k ≅ A^2_k has extra points corresponding to curves not visible as naive set-products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, W-valued points behave well; closed points of finite type k-schemes over algebraically closed k give expected behavior by Nullstellensatz. Also fibered products can break Noetherianness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Noetherianness warning for fibered products
rubrics_metrics.description: The fibered product of Noetherian schemes need not be Noetherian (example: tensor product Q ⊗_Q Q producing a non-Noetherian ring A with infinitely many points).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: But fibered products of finite type k-schemes over finite type k-schemes remain finite type over k (Exercise 9.2.D), so varieties avoid this pathology.
